\begin{table*}[t]
  \centering
  \small
  \caption{Embedding-space separability of human and generated text, by generator,
  register and prompt condition. Values are the cross-validated ROC AUC of a
  logistic-regression classifier trained to separate human from generated
  embeddings (\texttt{paraphrase-multilingual-mpnet-base-v2}); $0.5$ is chance and
  $1.0$ is perfect separability, so \emph{higher} means the generated text is
  easier to tell apart from human text. Every reported AUC is significant at
  $p<.001$ under a 1{,}000-run label permutation test (null mean AUC $\approx0.50$).
  GPT-5.2 and Mistral~3.2 are run on the full corpora ($n=170$ per class formal,
  $n=1{,}149$ informal); GPT-5.6 exists only as the 100-document quiz corpus
  ($n=100$, and $n=98$ for formal detector-evasive). Because cross-validated AUC
  rises with training-set size, the GPT-5.6 row is \emph{not} directly comparable
  down the column. Re-running the other two generators on the same 100 documents
  gives, for baseline / human-mimicking / detector-evasive: GPT-5.2
  $0.643/0.643/0.813$ (formal) and $0.886/0.898/0.935$ (informal); Mistral
  $0.935/0.925/0.909$ and $0.916/0.954/0.874$. Under that matched comparison
  GPT-5.6 remains the least separable generator in the informal register
  (${\approx}0.10$ AUC below GPT-5.2 on identical documents), whereas in the formal
  register it is \emph{more} separable than GPT-5.2 at baseline and
  human-mimicking, so the effect does not generalise across registers.}
  \label{tab:embedding-auc}
  \begin{tabular}{lllc}
    \toprule
    Generator & Register & Condition & Embedding CV ROC AUC \\
    \midrule
    \multirow{6}{*}{GPT-5.2}

    \cmidrule(l){2-4}

\begin{table*}[t]
  \centering
  \small
  \caption{Large-language-model-as-judge AI-text detection, by generator, register
  and prompt condition (all values are percentages). \emph{AI recall} is the share
  of generated items the judge flagged as AI. \emph{Human precision} is the share of
  the items the judge labelled \emph{human} that really are human, computed within
  each cell by pooling that cell's generated items with the register's $n=100$ human
  items; it therefore falls towards $50\%$ as recall falls, because undetected
  generated text accumulates in the ``human'' bin. All completed cells use $n=100$
  generated items per condition; the Gemini$\times$Mistral (informal) cells, formerly
  quota-limited to $n=90/89/89$, were completed on 2026-08-03.
  For reference, human-item specificity is Claude 100\%, DeepSeek 69\%, Gemini 100\%
  (formal, original corpus) and Claude 100\%, DeepSeek 86\%, Gemini 97\% (informal).
  The formal GPT-5.6 and Mistral cells are scored on the formatting-normalized formal
  corpus (markdown, section headings and the \texttt{Nyckelord} footer stripped
  uniformly from every source); on that corpus human specificity is Claude 100\% and
  DeepSeek 82\%, and those are the denominators behind their human-precision cells.
  $^\dagger$Claude's normalized formal run is scored on $n=88$--$90$ per cell rather
  than the full $n=100$; all six cells sit at $98$--$100\%$, so the remaining items
  cannot move them materially. \emph{n/a} marks the Gemini formal cells, which were
  never scored: \texttt{gemini-3.1-pro-preview} is capped at 250 requests/day on the
  available key, which did not permit a 998-item run inside the study period.
  \textbf{The formal GPT-5.2 row is not comparable with the GPT-5.6 and Mistral formal
  rows}: it is scored on the original, non-normalized corpus. On the normalized corpus
  DeepSeek scores $86\%$ pooled recall on the same GPT-5.2 documents versus $58\%$
  on the original, so the apparent jump from GPT-5.2 to GPT-5.6 in the DeepSeek formal
  column reflects corpus version (or provider drift), not generator. The informal GPT-5.2 baseline
  is the corrected GPT-5.2 column, not the gpt-4o-mini text (see
  \texttt{BASELINE\_PROVENANCE.md}).}
  \label{tab:llm-judge-detection-by-condition}
